newsitem.title: UK: Oil price set to slip, rally may reignite later.
newsitem.headline: Oil price set to slip, rally may reignite later.

text.p: Rising oil supplies should start outstripping global demand by spring and take the steam out of a torrid rally which has kept crude prices near six-year highs, analysts said on Monday.
But until then tight inventories of heating fuel in key consumer markets should keep a flame under oil prices.

Even though supply-demand fundamentals should dictate lower prices for the northern hemisphere spring, analysts say there is a good chance the rally will reignite later in the year when demand picks up.

However, when demand slows down to a seasonal low around April, the market should be awash with crude oil from extra non-OPEC production and renewed Iraqi exports to tip the balance back in buyers' favour, the analysts said.
"I think there will be multi-dollar drop in price," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, economist at Washington-based Petroleum Finance Corp (PFC). "Prices are going to fall before they go up again."
"Oil prices should return gradually to more normal ( lower) levels in the face of rising supply," said Mehdi Varzi at finance house Kleinwort Benson.
International benchmark Brent blend crude oil averaged $20.30 a barrel in 1996, up 20 per cent on the year and was trading at $24 on Monday.
Varzi expects Brent, which is produced in the North Sea, to average $20 a barrel in the first half of 1997. But PFC's Abduljabbar saw Brent below $20 by April or May.
Analysts said a recovery in the level of western oil stocks, would provide the key to lower prices after winter demand for heating oil tails off.
Inventories of crude oil and key refined oil products like heating oil fell in 1996 to their lowest levels in years in the major consuming markets in the United States and Europe.
The low stock levels combined with record high global demand to push oil prices late last year to their highest levels since 1991, stunning even the most bullish analyst price forecasts.
"Our figures tell us there will be a gradual build in crude stocks starting next year, 100,000 barrels per day in the first quarter and then one million bpd in the second," PFC's Abduljabbar said.

"The oil industry's continuing need to rebuild stocks ought to ensure oil prices do not weaken in the first quarter," said Leo Drollas at London's Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES). "However, the strength in oil prices could erode significantly during the second quarter, once storage tanks have been refilled to comfortable levels,"
Inventories hit rock bottom in October as oil companies fought for competitive advantage by cutting stocks to the bone.

But Iraq's return to the market under a limited United Nations oil-for-food exchange combined with new North Sea oilfield start-ups delayed from last year will allow stocks to stage a steady recovery.

"Iraqi oil and North Sea output will push global supplies to peak levels at the exact time when global demand falls to its lowest point for the year in April and May," Petrofinance Corp. said in a recent report.

Oil markets so far have easily absorbed Iraq's early exports under a U.N. deal which, at current prices, allows Baghdad some 500,000 barrels daily of sales over six months to raise funds for humanitarian aid.
Oil prices have the potential later this year to reignite fears about inflationary pressures in industrialised economies.
An extra two million barrels a day of world demand will take world oil consumption to 73.7 million bpd in 1997.
And if fast-rising non-OPEC supply plus an expected upward creep from oil cartel OPEC fails to match expectations Brent could challenge $25 again.

"Oil demand is growing in nearly all regions," said Varzi at Kleinwort Benson. "Demand is rising even in 'mature' oil markets (and) there are few signs of any appreciable slowdown ... in the developing economies."
The unpredictable Saddam Hussein might also surprise the oil market.
The Iraqi President could take action to scupper the U.N. oil sale deal which is up for renewal in mid-June.
"There is the possibility .... the deal will not be renewed in June -- perhaps by Saddam," said Drollas at the CGES.
